notes.title: Different evidence, different placement
notes.text: Manual-alphabet comparisons group the Czech sample with two-handed alphabets; Abner’s lexical-feature analysis places Czech among European samples. This is a difference in the compared subsystem, not proof that one entire-language genealogy is wrong.

notes.title: Compare lexical and manual-alphabet results
notes.text: The review describes Lithuanian and Polish manual alphabets as intermediate between Russian and Austrian groups. In the lexical analysis, Lithuanian clusters with eastern European samples while Polish is less resolved. Contact and different evidence can explain some differences.

notes.title: How to read sign-language evidence
notes.text: Manual alphabets encode fingerspelling; lexical-feature trees compare properties of vocabulary. Neither should be silently substituted for an established cognate-based genealogy. Catalog categories are navigation, not a proposed ancestor of all sign languages.

notes.title: Language emergence
notes.text: Research on Nicaraguan Sign Language examines the emergence of structure across cohorts. It does not establish descent from the spoken language of the surrounding community.

notes.title: Design account and proposed influence
notes.text: Ledyard (1966) proposes a Phags-pa connection for selected consonant forms. Lee (2013), pp. 40–42, criticizes that proposal: the selected basic letters differ from the design account in Hunminjeongeum haerye. Lee favors the documented articulatory design account. The proposed connection is disputed, not established descent of the whole system.

notes.title: Competing origin accounts
notes.text: Unicode describes an ultimately Semitic, probably Aramaic origin. Pillai (2023) instead proposes a hybrid drawing on Aramaic, Phoenician and Greek. The latter is a published hypothesis, not a settled replacement for other accounts.

notes.title: Writing signs is not language ancestry
notes.text: SignWriting is used to write sign languages; HamNoSys is a transcription system for signs. Sharing a notation does not make two sign languages genealogically related. No universal language-to-notation usage edges are inferred.

limitations: Complete imports of the identified catalog snapshots, not a complete inventory of all world languages or scripts.
All 344 Glottolog Sign Language-category records are preserved, including families, dialects and non-genealogical categories.
Script catalog membership is much broader than the manually reviewed historical relationship set. A script with no edge has an unreviewed or unasserted placement, not a certified independent origin.
SIL-local IDs are preserved and never fuzzy-merged with ISO codes. Possible duplicate concepts remain source-specific.
Historical descent, graphic influence, sample identity and script usage are distinct relations. No global common ancestor is asserted.

English and French catalog labels and all Glottolog aliases are retained. Verified native names are sparse; script glyph samples are not autonyms. Sign-language self-names generally need video or sign notation and have not been fabricated.
Only selected source-backed disagreements are reviewed. No claim that every competing publication is incorporated.
Abner consensus branch lengths and posterior annotations are retained in JSON/XML; no time-scaled visual or posterior sample inference. Two European runs are replicates, not independent papers.
